newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China warns of cyanide poisoning in southern rivers.
newsitem.headline: China warns of cyanide poisoning in southern rivers.

text.p: Authorities in southern China on Wednesday warned of cyanide poisoning in river waters after a truck carrying the toxic chemical plunged into a tributary of the busy Pearl River, which flows into the South China Sea.
"The water has definitely been polluted. There were dead fish in our samples," an Environmental Protection Bureau official told a Hong Kong television station from Wuzhou in Guangxi province.
"We are taking hourly samples and the results will be given to authorities," he said.
The official told the television station potassium cyanide had spilled into the Gui river after a truck carrying 200 drums of it plunged into the water late on Tuesday.
Three of the drums were missing and 700 kg (1,540 pounds) of the chemical may have entered the river, he said.
The Gui is a tributary of the Pearl River, which flows through heavily populated Guangdong province and into the South China Sea near Hong Kong and Macau.
Potassium cyanide -- used in the electroplating industry and in the extraction of gold and silver -- dissolves in water and is toxic, a chemist at a Hong Kong government laboratory said.
"It's a very toxic chemical," senior chemist S.K. Choi told Reuters, but added that the enormous flow rate of the Pearl River would "have a very large dilution effect".

Several Hong Kong television stations showed scenes from Wuzhou of workers with rubber gloves dragging dozens of dented green drums from the murky Gui. Many of the drums had their tops missing, revealing white palm-sized pellets.
Some of the workers squatted by the river, scooping up floating pellets with plastic containers.

The municipal government of Zhuhai in Guangdong province posted emergency notices informing residents of pollution in nearby rivers and advised them against drinking the water, one Hong Kong television station reported.
But a Zhuhai official told the station there was no evidence of contamination in the lower streams.
The spill has raised fears in Macau, 200 km (125 miles) downriver from the accident, prompting the Portuguese-run enclave's water supply company to shut off the pipes to all water coming from China.
Macau, which receives most of its tap water from across the border in Zhuhai, said its eight million cubic metres of reserves would last for at least 45 days.
Supermarkets in central Macau reported a 20 percent rise in sales of bottled water since the accident was first reported on Tuesday evening.
Hong Kong government officials said the territory's water supply was not in jeopardy but that produce coming from southern China would be tested.

Choi, the government chemist, said the laboratory was expecting samples of water from the Pearl River to arrive for analysis. "It's just a precautionary measure -- not that we expect there will be any acute toxicity," he said.
